quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

entry.rationale: Primary search: keyword search of the Rowan County probate records for the surname Voss across the whole window, not a browse by year. The Rowan probate index is name-searchable but only partly name-indexed (loc_001), so a keyword search is more reliable than browsing. The window runs from Caroline's birth in 1839 to about 60 years after it, because a father's estate could be probated long after her birth. It is not capped at her marriage of about 1858 (tree fact F2, source S1), which names no parents. A will or estate file naming Caroline or her siblings would be direct evidence of parentage.

Fallback to item 1: if the keyword search returns nothing, browse the image groups of the Rowan County probate dockets year by year. This statewide probate collection is browse-only, so it is read by image rather than searched by name, and it reaches files the partial name index misses.

Co-equal statewide estate-file index, searched by surname Voss with Rowan County as the place. It is name-searchable and may hold Rowan estate files that the county probate index does not surface. Searched alongside item 1, not as a fallback.

Mortality schedules list deaths in the year before each census. A Voss death in Rowan County in that span would date the father's death and point to the probate year to search in item 1. This is a lead to the estate, not proof that the decedent was Caroline's father.

The 1850 census is the first to name every member of a household, and Caroline (about 11) should appear in her parents' home. It names her father's household and age, but not relationship to the head before 1880, so it shows co-residence only. It supports the link to a father named in a probate record and suggests which estate to test.

Parents' marriage before Caroline's birth. A Rowan marriage record would confirm the couple as a unit and may name the mother's maiden name, which is not in the tree. Her marriage of about 1858 (S1) names no parents, so it cannot serve. This record corroborates a father named in a probate record but does not by itself prove that Caroline is their child.

Finding-aid check on the Voss family's burials. The cemetery inscription index may give a father's death or burial year and a probate date. It is a lead to be tested against the probate file, not evidence of parentage.

Guardianship or court papers for a minor Caroline after her father's death, which would run before her marriage of about 1858. Browse-only, so read by image. A guardian's petition or bond names the minor children and the decedent, which tests parentage. Its date window is set by Caroline's minority, not by the probate window in item 1.

output.text_response:
Here is the research plan created for question q\_001 — **"Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. about 1845, d. 1908)?"**

---

## Plan pl\_002 — Parentage of Patrick Flynn

**What the tree already holds:**
- Patrick (I1): born ~1845 in Ireland, died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (cites a death certificate, S3, but it has not been read for parental information).
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born ~1818 in Ireland. A parent–child relationship (R1) links him to Patrick, citing the 1850 census, 1860 census, and death certificate — but none of those assertions have been extracted yet.
- 1850 census log entry: Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household in Schuylkill. The parent–child link is inferred from position/surname, not stated in the record.
- **Note:** The objective says Patrick was born in Pennsylvania, but the tree and 1850 census say Ireland — two plan items test this discrepancy.

---

## Ten Plan Items, in Execution Order

| # | ID | Type | Target |
|---|-----|------|--------|
| 1 | pli_004 | Vital record | Pennsylvania death certificates 1906–1908, FamilySearch — what does the certificate say about his parents? |
| 2 | pli_005 | Vital record | Patrick's marriage record 1865–1908, FamilySearch — may name his parents |
| 3 | pli_006 | Census | 1860 Schuylkill census, FamilySearch — is Patrick listed as Thomas's son? |
| 4 | pli_007 | Census | 1870–1880 Schuylkill censuses, FamilySearch — track the household and whether Thomas is alive |
| 5 | pli_008 | Vital record | Thomas Flynn's marriage(s) 1835–1850, FamilySearch — a remarriage changes the mother's surname |
| 6 | pli_009 | Church | Patrick's baptism 1840–1851, FamilySearch — flagged: may not exist if he was born in Ireland |
| 7 | pli_010 | Cemetery | Thomas Flynn's death and burial 1850–1900, FamilySearch |
| 8 | pli_011 | Probate | Thomas Flynn's will or administration 1845–1900, Schuylkill County Register of Wills (browse by image) |
| 9 | pli_012 | Military | Pennsylvania Civil War volunteer and GAR records 1861–1865, FamilySearch — settles birthplace |
| 10 | pli_013 | Church/FAN | Other Flynn children and their sponsors in Schuylkill church records 1835–1865, FamilySearch — required for a parentage question |

---

**Gap noted:** If the baptism turns out to be in Ireland, a locality survey for Ireland will be needed (not yet run).

**Next step:** Search the Pennsylvania death certificate for Patrick Flynn — the most likely single record to name his parents — followed by his marriage record.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's Pennsylvania death certificate (death 1908, Schuylkill County) is the first candidate for naming his parents. The tree's ParentChild relationship cites a Pennsylvania death certificate source, but no assertion from it is in research.json, so what it states about the parents is unverified. The collection is name-searchable. loc_001 notes that statewide civil registration began in 1906, so a 1908 death has a state certificate. The certificate may also give a birthplace bearing on the conflict between the tree (Ireland) and the question framing (Pennsylvania).

Patrick Flynn's own marriage entry, which may name his father and mother as well as the bride. Search the county marriage collection and the civil marriage collection, both name-searchable. A marriage entry is a route to parents independent of the baptism register. It does not establish the parents by itself.

The 1850 census (logged as positive) lists Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, but states no relationship; the child-of-head link is only inferred from household position and shared surname. The 1860 census names each person's relationship to the head, so this household is the first test of whether Patrick is Thomas's son. The tree's ParentChild relationship cites a 1860 census source that no assertion in research.json extracts.

The 1870 and 1880 censuses test the household after 1860: whether Patrick is still listed as a son of Thomas, whether Thomas is alive, and whether a widow with the same children appears. The 1880 census names relationship to the head. Patrick's age in 1870 and 1880 should match the roughly 1845 birth estimate.

A dedicated item for Thomas Flynn's marriage or marriages, not Patrick's. Such a record confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's maiden name, and corroborates the father's identity by its date relative to Patrick's birth. Search the compiled, civil and church marriage collections, all name-searchable. Thomas (b. about 1818, Ireland) may have married more than once. Each marriage record for Thomas must be searched, because a surname on one record may be a prior married name. A marriage alone does not show that Patrick is Thomas's child.

Patrick's baptism or christening, which may name both parents. The tree gives his birth as about 1845 in Ireland, while the question framing says Pennsylvania, and the 1850 census gives birthplace Ireland. If he was born in Ireland, a Schuylkill baptism may not exist, and the Irish parish is outside loc_001. Search the births and christenings and the county church collections, both name-searchable, and note in any hit whether the parish is in Pennsylvania. Irish baptism would need a separate locality survey.

Thomas Flynn's death and burial entries. Burial entries often name a spouse, children or an origin parish, and they do not depend on a baptism register. Search the deaths and burials collection and the cemetery collection, both name-searchable. The 1850-1880 mortality schedule is not planned here, because the 1850 census already placed the household. Thomas's death date is unknown and is sought here.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration file, held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills from 1811 (loc_001). A will or estate filing may name Patrick as a son and heir, which would be direct parentage evidence. The window runs from the 1850 census to the upper end of Thomas's plausible lifespan, because the death date is unknown. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's dockets, not a name search. The FamilySearch probate collection is the first route; the county office is the fallback if the browse fails.

Patrick would be 16 to 20 during the Civil War, so a Pennsylvania volunteer register or a GAR membership record may exist. These name-searchable records often give age and birthplace, which bears on the Ireland-versus-Pennsylvania conflict in the tree. They are not expected to name parents, so this item tests birthplace, not parentage.

FAN item: baptisms, marriages and burials of other Flynn children and their sponsors in Schuylkill County church records. A baptism of a sibling naming Thomas and the same mother would be direct parentage evidence for Patrick, and a sponsor who is a relative would point to the family unit. Search the county church collection, name-searchable, for Flynn entries with the same parents, then check godparents against the 1850 and 1860 households.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage entry, which may name his father and mother as well as the bride. Search the county marriage collection and the civil marriage collection, both name-searchable. A marriage entry is a route to parents independent of the baptism register. It does not establish the parents by itself.

The 1850 census (logged as positive) lists Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household, but states no relationship; the child-of-head link is only inferred from household position and shared surname. The 1860 census names each person's relationship to the head, so this household is the first test of whether Patrick is Thomas's son. The tree's ParentChild relationship cites a 1860 census source that no assertion in research.json extracts.

The 1870 and 1880 censuses test the household after 1860: whether Patrick is still listed as a son of Thomas, whether Thomas is alive, and whether a widow with the same children appears. The 1880 census names relationship to the head. Patrick's age in 1870 and 1880 should match the roughly 1845 birth estimate.

A dedicated item for Thomas Flynn's marriage or marriages, not Patrick's. Such a record confirms the couple as a unit, may give the mother's maiden name, and corroborates the father's identity by its date relative to Patrick's birth. Search the compiled, civil and church marriage collections, all name-searchable. Thomas (b. about 1818, Ireland) may have married more than once. Each marriage record for Thomas must be searched, because a surname on one record may be a prior married name. A marriage alone does not show that Patrick is Thomas's child.

Patrick's baptism or christening, which may name both parents. The tree gives his birth as about 1845 in Ireland, while the question framing says Pennsylvania, and the 1850 census gives birthplace Ireland. If he was born in Ireland, a Schuylkill baptism may not exist, and the Irish parish is outside loc_001. Search the births and christenings and the county church collections, both name-searchable, and note in any hit whether the parish is in Pennsylvania. Irish baptism would need a separate locality survey.

Thomas Flynn's death and burial entries. Burial entries often name a spouse, children or an origin parish, and they do not depend on a baptism register. A baptism of a sibling naming Thomas and the same mother would be direct parentage evidence for Patrick, and a sponsor who is a relative would point to the family unit. ---

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?
items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

entry.rationale: Parents' marriage: Thomas Flynn (about 1818, born Ireland, head of household in the 1850 and 1860 census entries) is not yet linked to any wife in the project, and no record names the mother. Search Pennsylvania Church Marriages and Pennsylvania County Marriages (both name-searchable) under Thomas Flynn for the bride and her parents. The marriage supplies her maiden name only if it was her first marriage, so pair it with items 3 and 4 to test for an earlier marriage. The marriage can corroborate parentage by date but cannot establish that Patrick is their child on its own.

Sibling and household baptisms: Pennsylvania Births and Christenings (name-searchable) for Flynn children baptized in Schuylkill parishes, whose entries may name Thomas Flynn and his wife as parents. Patrick was born in Ireland, so his own baptism is unlikely to appear here. Roman Catholic sacramental registers stayed with the parish and diocese rather than the county (locality quirk), so any index hit must be checked against the parish register image. This is a FAN item: a sibling's baptism naming the same parents is direct parentage evidence for Patrick.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration file, held by the county Register of Wills (locality quirk: available from 1811). The window is sized to Thomas's own lifespan, not the research window: he was alive in 1860 and could have died up to about age 80, so the window runs to about 1900. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son, and naming a wife, would be direct evidence. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so this is an image-by-image browse of the Schuylkill dockets, not a name search.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage: Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages (both name-searchable). Marriage applications and parish entries sometimes name the groom's parents, which would test the Thomas Flynn link from a second record. It also gives the bride's family, a FAN lead, and it is the record that would reveal whether Patrick had a Flynn wife other than the one named by the 1908 death certificate's informant chain.

Burials of Thomas Flynn, his wife and any Flynn children, in Pennsylvania Cemetery Records and Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials (both name-searchable). A burial or stone can give an age that tests Thomas's birth near 1818, name a spouse, and show a family plot that places Patrick with his parents. Patrick's own 1908 burial is also here, to match the family plot. Burials in Catholic parishes may appear in the parish register instead, which is held by the parish.

Patrick Flynn's estate file at the Schuylkill Register of Wills (browse-only). The window is sized to the estate's own timing after his March 1908 death. An administration can name his heirs, which are FAN leads (siblings or a parent still living), and may state the relationship of his heirs to him. The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father, but its informant was a son-in-law (secondary), so an estate file that names the same father would be independent corroboration.

Mortality schedules, not a population census: Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules (name-searchable) for deaths in the Thomas Flynn household in the 1850, 1860, 1870 and 1880 enumeration years. A death of a mother or sibling there would name the household and a relationship-to-deceased, and would show the wife's death date, which bears on any remarriage. The population census items were completed earlier and are not repeated.

FAN item on the son-in-law James Brown, who gave the 1908 death certificate's father information. A county marriage record for Brown and Patrick's daughter (County Marriages, name-searchable) may name the bride's parents and residence, which shows whether Brown was close enough to the family to be a reliable informant on Patrick's parentage. Treat it as a lead on Brown's knowledge, not as evidence of parentage.

Mode taken: create a new plan (Add-new mode). The previous plan for q_001, pl_002, had both of its items closed (the 1860 census and the 1908 death certificate), so I left it as the record of what was done. The question is still only "probable" (ps_001), with no proof of parentage yet.

I wrote **pl_003** as the active plan for q_001: "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

**Survey of what the tree already holds:**
- Patrick Flynn (I1): birth ~1845, Ireland (1850 census); death 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, PA (death certificate). His parent link to Thomas Flynn rests on the 1908 death certificate and the 1850/1860 census households.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): birth ~1818, Ireland. No wife, marriage, or death is recorded in the tree, so the mother is unknown.
- The 1908 death certificate names Thomas as father. Its informant was James Brown, a son-in-law, so that is secondary evidence. The proof summary also notes a birthplace conflict: census says Ireland, the death certificate says Pennsylvania.

**Plan items, in execution order:**
1. **pli_006, church marriage (1835–1846), FamilySearch.** Thomas Flynn's marriage to the mother, to get her maiden name and her parents. Pennsylvania Church Marriages and County Marriages are both name-searchable.
2. **pli_007, church baptisms (1835–1870), FamilySearch.** Sibling baptisms in Schuylkill parishes naming Thomas and his wife. This is the FAN item. Catholic registers are held by the parish or diocese, so index hits need checking against the register image.
3. **pli_008, probate (1860–1900), county Register of Wills.** Thomas Flynn's will or administration, naming Patrick and a wife. The collection is browse-only, so this is an image-by-image browse. The window runs to about 1900 because Thomas was alive in 1860.
4. **pli_009, church and county marriages (1865–1900).** Patrick's own marriage, which may name his parents and gives the bride's family.
5. **pli_010, cemetery and burials (1850–1910).** Burials and stones for Thomas, his wife and children, and Patrick's 1908 burial, to test ages and family plot.
6. **pli_011, probate (1908–1915).** Patrick's estate file. Its heirs are FAN leads, and it may independently name his father.
7. **pli_012, mortality schedules (1850–1880).** Deaths in the Thomas household, which may show the wife's death. This is not a population census, so it is not a repeat of the census work.
8. **pli_013, church and county marriages (1880–1910), FAN.** Patrick's daughter's marriage to James Brown, to test how close Brown was to the family and whether he is a reliable informant.

All eight items are `planned`. None has a fallback link.

**Things to note:**
- I did not plan the 1870, 1880 or 1900 census. You said the censuses were done, and the proof summary lists them as unsearched. Tell me if you want them added.
- Patrick's own baptism is unlikely to be in a Pennsylvania collection, because he was born in Ireland. Item 2 covers the siblings instead.
- Nothing in the project states that the mother had a previous marriage. Items 1, 3 and 4 are designed to check for one.

Would you like me to start executing this plan? The first search is the parents' marriage (pli_006), which goes to search-records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Use Pennsylvania, County Marriages (name-searchable) first, then Pennsylvania, Church Marriages (name-searchable) for Catholic parishes. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so the record sits in the county, not under Berks or Northampton.

FAN item: baptisms of Thomas Flynn's other children. A sibling's baptism names the same parents and can state the mother's maiden name. Pennsylvania civil birth registration did not begin until 1906, so church baptisms are the only early birth record. Use Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings (name-searchable), matching by parish and parent name, since Catholic sacramental registers are held by the parish under the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Patrick's own baptism is not assumed to be indexed.

FAN item: Thomas Flynn's estate file held by the county Register of Wills (probate available from 1811 in this county). An estate file or will can name Patrick and other heirs as sons, and the inventory and administrator bond name neighbours and creditors. The window runs from Patrick's birth to about 72 years after Thomas's birth (~1818), the creator's plausible lifespan. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills dockets, not a name search.

Fallback to the probate browse if the estate file is not found: Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds (name-searchable) indexes Thomas Flynn as grantor, grantee, or testator. Deeds recite adjoining landowners, who are FAN neighbours and often kin, and a deed by Thomas to a named son or a release by heirs can state the family relationship.

FAN item: burials of Thomas Flynn and his wife, and of Flynn family members in Schuylkill cemeteries. Use Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records (name-searchable) and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials (name-searchable).

Census-based test, not direct proof. Use United States, Census, 1880 (name-searchable). The 1850 and 1860 enumerations do not state relationships, so this is the first census that can settle the question.

Remaining census gap: the 1870 census is a separate enumeration that can show whether Thomas's household still included Patrick, and whether a mother or other relative lived there. It does not state relationships, so it corroborates the 1850 and 1860 placement rather than proving parentage. Use United States, Census, 1870 (name-searchable).

Patrick's own household in 1900: the 1900 census records each person's parents' birthplaces and whether a mother is living, and it may show an aged parent or a relative in Patrick's home. Use United States, Census, 1900 (name-searchable). This item tests Patrick's household links and does not name his parents directly.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.

The Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds collection is name-searchable. Deeds and leases in the county recorder's office, from 1811 onward, may name Michael with an occupation or residence. The window starts four years before the 1882 residence to catch any earlier purchase or lease that would show the move was planned.

Pennsylvania naturalization collections are name-searchable. The tree does not record Civil War service, so this is a conditional check: if Michael served, a volunteer register may give a residence, and a later pension or GAR record could give the county of residence after the war. Item 8 is low priority and can be skipped if it finds nothing.

Company payroll, colliery employment, and mine inspectors' records would show a named miner at a particular colliery and would test the work-driven move directly. No such collection appeared in the locality survey or the collection search, so the holding repository is not yet identified. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845) would be about 35 in 1880, and Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) about 62 if living. The 1880 census is the first federal schedule to state each person's relationship to the head of household, so it can directly test the parent-child reading that the 1850 and 1860 household placements only suggest (ps_001 rates both as indirect). Search the United States, Census, 1880 collection (name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn with a Thomas Flynn household in Schuylkill County where Patrick is listed as son. Record the birthplace given, because the 1850 and 1860 censuses say Ireland while the 1908 death certificate says Pennsylvania (c_001).

The 1870 census is the next federal schedule after the 1860 household placement (log_004, Patrick age 15 with Thomas Flynn). It does not state relationships, so it can corroborate co-residence only, but it tracks Patrick as an adult of about 25 and shows whether he still lives with a Thomas Flynn or has left. Search the United States, Census, 1870 collection (name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn born about 1845 and Thomas Flynn born about 1818 in Ireland, both in Schuylkill County. Note whether the birthplace stays Ireland.

The 1900 census is the last federal schedule before Patrick's 1908 death and states relationship to the head of household, as the 1880 census does. Patrick would be about 55 and Thomas, if living, about 82. Search the United States, Census, 1900 collection (name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn born about 1845 in Pennsylvania or Ireland, and for a household headed by Thomas Flynn with Patrick as son or as a boarder or relative. If Thomas is absent, a Patrick Flynn household in Schuylkill County may show the father's death as a widowed or single-headed household. Also note the birth year and birthplace recorded.

A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, distinct from the census searches. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable) and Pennsylvania Marriages, 1709-1940 (name-searchable) should be searched for a Thomas Flynn marriage before Patrick's birth, around 1835-1846. The marriage would confirm the couple as a unit and may give the mother's maiden name, but only if it was her first marriage; a second marriage would need a separate search. It corroborates the father but does not by itself prove that Patrick is their child.

FAN item. Search the 1870 census in Schuylkill County for James Brown, the son-in-law who gave the death certificate informant statement (log_005), and for neighbors of the Thomas Flynn household in 1860 (log_004). A Brown household that includes Patrick, or a neighbor who lists Thomas Flynn and Patrick in the same district, would give a second, independent placement in a household that does not depend on the surname alone. This tests the death certificate's informant and whether Brown knew Patrick's family.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

facts.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is already cited to a Pennsylvania death certificate (S3) in the tree, but that certificate has not been read for its parent fields. Re-read the existing certificate image for the father's and mother's names and birthplaces, then search Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (name-searchable) for a second copy or transcription. A 1908 certificate is a state record (statewide registration began 1906) and often names parents, which is direct parentage evidence.

The 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (log_001, dwelling 84) is documented, but the 1850 census states no relationships. The United States Census, 1880 (name-searchable) is the first census to record each person's relationship to the head, so it can test whether Patrick is Thomas's son. Patrick would be about 35 and Thomas about 62 if both were living.

The United States Census, 1860 (name-searchable) shows whether Thomas Flynn's household still held Patrick and names the wife, who is not named in any record in the project. Relationships are not stated in 1860, so this item confirms co-residence and the wife's given name, not parentage.

Dedicated parents'-marriage item. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (both name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn with a wife, dated before Patrick's birth around 1845. A marriage record supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, and it corroborates a father but does not by itself prove that Patrick is their child. Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (name-searchable) is a companion check for the parish marriage. Patrick's birth in Ireland per the tree may mean the marriage took place in Ireland; that jurisdiction is not yet surveyed.

Companion item for the mother's identity. Her earlier marriages are not yet known, so search for her by each surname she is recorded under in the 1850 and 1860 households and in the parents' marriage record, across Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and the Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 (both name-searchable). A death or burial that names a husband or a maiden name can show whether the marriage found in item 4 was her first. The surname typed into a search asserts nothing about her birth name.

Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn and the wife's burial in Schuylkill cemeteries. A burial may give a birth year and birthplace, and a family plot can show children buried beside the parents, which is FAN evidence. Thomas was born about 1818, so his burial could fall anywhere from the 1850s onward.

Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811, a primary source that names heirs. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of Thomas Flynn's estate and any estate of the wife, not a name search. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan (born about 1818), so it runs to 1900. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son would be direct evidence of parentage.

Schuylkill County Orphans' Court kept estate dockets and distributions, and guardianship papers when a minor heir was involved. This is the fallback for item 7 if the Register of Wills images cannot be browsed. The date window is sized to Thomas's lifespan and to the children's minority. A distribution list naming the heirs is direct parentage evidence. Access is unknown, so the researcher may need to visit or request copies.

FAN item. Search Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable) for the children of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County and for sponsors. A sibling's baptism names the same parents, and a sponsor can be a relative. Because the tree gives Patrick's birth in Ireland, Patrick's own baptism is unlikely to be here. Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county, and access to those is unknown.

FAN item. The 1850 United States Census (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn's household is already found (log_001), but the dwellings next to dwelling 84 have not been examined. Neighbours with the same Irish birthplace may be kin, a sibling household, or the source of the wife's name. Examining the adjoining dwellings is a FAN test of whether Thomas came with relatives.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The marriage dates the union against Patrick's birth c.1845 but does not by itself show that Patrick is their child. Name-searchable (Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991).

FAN item. A sibling baptism naming Thomas Flynn and the mother would give direct parentage evidence for Patrick's siblings and would name the mother. Patrick's own baptism is not in Pennsylvania records (he was born in Ireland per the 1850 and 1860 censuses). Name-searchable (Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950), and the parish registers are held by the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county, per loc_001.

Thomas would be about 82 in 1900, so a household with Patrick as son or as a boarder would show the link late in life. Name-searchable (United States, Census, 1900). Included so the census series runs to the end of the subject's window, as ps_001 notes the 1900 census is unsearched.

Patrick's own burial entry, a second informant to the death certificate that names Thomas Flynn as father (pli_005, log_005). A church burial record is kept separately from the civil death certificate and may name parents from a different informant. Name-searchable (Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999).

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Pennsylvania, Carbon County, Jim Thorpe, Cemetery Records, 1747-2007
Pennsylvania, Crew Lists arriving at Erie, 1952-1957
Pennsylvania, Eastern District Court, Naturalization Records, 1795-1952
Pennsylvania, Grand Army of the Republic Membership Records, 1865-1936
Pennsylvania, Huntingdon County, Delayed Birth Records, 1800-1935
Pennsylvania, Middle District Court, Naturalization Records, 1901-1992
Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County, Schuylkill Haven, Funeral Home Obituary Cards, 1914-2007
Pennsylvania, Wayne County, Court of Common Pleas, Naturalization Records, 1799-1906
Pennsylvania, World War II Draft Registration Cards, 1940-1945
United States City and Business Directories, ca. 1749 - ca. 1990
United States, Social Security Death Index

entry.rationale: Baptism entries naming Bridget Halloran as mother and John Doyle as father are the most direct evidence for each child. Bridget was born about 1838 and bore about nine children (1900 census, log_002), so the birth window runs from her marriage to John Doyle (undated; 1858-1866 assumed) to about 1882. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950, is name-searchable. Pre-1906 births have no state registration (loc_001), so the baptism is the main birth record. Search by both parents' names, allowing Irish spelling variants (Halloran, Halaran; Doyle, Doil). The register is kept by the Catholic parish, not the county, so an indexed hit must be checked against the parish image.

Fallback to pli_001. If the name-indexed baptism search finds nothing, the Schuylkill church-records image group is browse-only (German and English text), so this is an image-by-image browse of the Catholic register pages for 1858-1882. Loc_001 notes that anthracite-region church films are browse-only, and the register is held by the parish, so a browse can find an entry the index omitted. Look for the Doyle surname and any entry naming Bridget as mother.

Full-text co-occurrence search, run unscoped with the two names as separate terms (John Doyle and Bridget Halloran), routed to the search-full-text skill. It is a fallback to pli_001 for when the parish entries are not name-indexed or the names are transcribed with variants. It can surface a baptism, a sponsor's entry or a burial that names both parents, which the surname index would miss.

Parents' marriage: John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, Schuylkill County, before the first child. Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976, and County Marriages, 1775-1991, are both name-searchable. The marriage confirms the couple as a unit, dates the start of the child-bearing window, and names Bridget's maiden surname Halloran. Ellen Doyle's marriage (log_003) names John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as her parents, so the couple is established. Remarriage is possible, so a search in these records for any earlier husband of Bridget should not be ruled out.

US Census 1870 household of John and Bridget Doyle, Schuylkill County. The census is name-searchable. It names every member of the household, so it can place children at home with both parents in the 1870 enumeration. Relationship to head is not recorded before 1880, so the children are linked to the couple by household co-residence and age only, not by the census's stated relationship.

US Census 1880 for the Doyle household, or for Bridget as a widow with children under the surname Doyle. The census is name-searchable and records each person's relationship to head. It can show which children were alive and living with Bridget after John's death, and it can name children living elsewhere in the county as part of the household or as boarders. Compare with the 1870 household (pli_005).

Mortality schedules for 1870 and 1880 record deaths in the year before each census. Bridget's 1900 entry reports 9 children born and 2 living, so about seven children died before 1900, and a mortality schedule can name a child who died in that window. The United States Mortality Schedule, 1850-1880, and Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, are both name-searchable. A death listed here names the household and the child's age, which can tie a child to the couple.

John Doyle's death and burial, and any family plot naming his children, dated from the marriage to the 1900 census (window sized to John's own lifespan, about 1830 to 1900). Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950, are both name-searchable. Pre-1906 death records are not in the state register (loc_001), so the burial and cemetery entries are the main source. A family lot can name the children who died young, which the 1900 count implies.

John Doyle's estate file (will or administration) at the Schuylkill County Register of Wills. Probate names heirs and minor children, and it often names guardians for minors, which tests who the children were. Loc_001 says probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811, so the county is the holding repository. The Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994, collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's probate docket. Window is sized to John's lifespan (about 1830 to 1900), not to the subject's, because the file is filed by his estate.

Bridget's own death, burial or obituary, after her 1900 census entry and her 1879 remarriage to Martin Kearney (log_001). Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, is name-searchable and the Schuylkill Haven funeral home obituary cards (1914-2007) are name-searchable. A death or obituary often lists surviving children by name, and it would cover children who survived past 1900. Search under Bridget Kearney, Bridget Doyle and Bridget Halloran.

The 1900 Kearney household (log_002 gave Bridget 9 children, 2 living). Check the full enumeration for children living in the household under the Doyle or Kearney surname, and for children of any age living elsewhere in the county. The 1900 census is name-searchable. The image has already been read once, so this search is about finding any listed child by name in other households.

FAN item: Ellen Doyle's own marriage (log_003) and its witnesses and sponsors. The entry names her parents, John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, and the witnesses at her wedding are often siblings or close relatives, so they may be other children of the couple. Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991, is name-searchable. Search for Ellen Doyle as bride, then record every witness and the parents' names as leads to test against the baptism and census results.

**Question (q_001):** Using Kentucky death certificates, what were the date and place of death of Elijah Wilkins (b. c. 1814, Muhlenberg County, Kentucky)?

| pli_006 | Muhlenberg County court order books, 1799–1901 | Browse-only | Fallback for administrator appointments |

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

entry.rationale: Subject Anna Margaretha Bauer's birth is recorded only as 1792 in Württemberg (tree fact F1, no day or parish). Her baptism is the first record that can name both parents. Search the collection Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (collection 1473000, name-searchable) on Anna Margaretha Bauer, and also on Margaretha alone, because the locality guide notes that children with two given names were often called by the second (FamilySearch Wiki: Germany Naming Customs). No parish is known yet, so search the surname with the year window and verify any hit against the register image.

Parentage question needs a dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. Their marriage in Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) should predate the 1792 birth; it confirms the couple as a unit and can give the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage. Her parents are unknown, so search the Bauer surname as the groom's name with Margaretha as the bride's given name across the window. The window starts before 1792 because the mother's age at the birth is unknown.

Sibling and FAN check. Other Bauer children baptised in the same register between about 1780 and 1800 would name the same parents, and their baptism sponsors (godparents) are the subject's relatives and associates. Search Germany, Births and Baptisms, 1558-1898 (collection 1473000, name-searchable) on the surname Bauer for children whose parents' given names match any candidate found in items 1 and 2, and record each sponsor's name for the FAN review.

Remarriage check. If the mother named in item 2 married more than once, the marriage record that gives her maiden name may be a later one, so every marriage she is found in must be tested. Search Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) on the bride's given name Margaretha with each surname found in items 1 to 3, and note any entry where the bride is named as a widow.

The subject's own death or burial entry is planned because her baptism may not survive or may not be reachable: the register start date for the birth parish is unknown, so the baptism cannot be assumed to exist. Death and burial entries often state an age, a home parish or a birthplace. Search Germany, Births and Baptisms and the Bauer surname in death or burial registers for women named Anna Margaretha with an age consistent with a 1792 birth.

The subject's own marriage entry is planned because it is a second route to her origin. Marriage entries often name the bride's father and home parish. Search Germany Marriages, 1558-1929 (collection 1473009, name-searchable) on Anna Margaretha Bauer as bride, across the years she could have married.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.question: Where was Patrick Flynn in the 1850 census?
items.rationale: The 1850 census is the earliest enumeration where Patrick would appear by name (age ~5). Locating him in a household identifies candidate parents.

search_stop.justification: Searched 1850 census for Schuylkill County on FamilySearch (indexed and browse), Ancestry (indexed), and MyHeritage (indexed). All three returned the same household. No other Patrick Flynn of matching age found in the county.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Yes — Patrick Flynn located in a specific 1850 household, answering the question.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: Three major repositories searched (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage). No additional known indexes of the 1850 Schuylkill County census exist.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: FamilySearch provides the original census image; Ancestry index is derivative but confirmed consistent.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: FamilySearch (original) and Ancestry (derivative) both return the same household. Two access paths, one underlying original.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: Yes — FamilySearch provides original census image with indeterminate-quality information.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: No conflicts on the 1850 census placement question.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low — all three repositories agree, and no competing Patrick Flynn of matching age exists in the county.

items.notes: Found Patrick Flynn age 5 in household of Thomas Flynn, dwelling 84, Schuylkill Co. Three other Flynn results examined — ages and locations don't match.
Ancestry index confirms same household. Transcription matches FamilySearch except Ancestry reads dwelling as 84, FamilySearch as 84 — consistent.
MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.

facts.informant: Unknown household member reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. The household member who provided the name is unknown. Proximity is 'unknown' rather than 'household_member' because for names specifically, the enumerator may have read a sign, heard a neighbor, or made an assumption — the name fact doesn't necessarily require active reporting the way age/birthplace does.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn or wife)
facts.informant_bias_notes: Age and birthplace require active reporting by a household member — someone had to tell the enumerator these facts. Proximity is 'household_member' rather than 'unknown' because these facts could only come from someone in the household.

facts.informant: Census enumerator (witness to residence by visiting the dwelling)
facts.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

facts.value: Listed in household of Thomas Flynn (head), position consistent with child
facts.informant: Inferred from household structure — no explicit informant for relationships in 1850 census
facts.informant_bias_notes: 1850 census does not state relationships; this assertion is inferred from household position and shared surname, not directly reported by any informant. The relationship is indirect evidence constructed by the researcher, not information provided by a census informant.

facts.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
facts.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

facts.informant: Ancestry transcriber (derivative of census enumerator)
facts.informant_bias_notes: Derivative index — transcription errors possible
