entry.rationale: Patrick's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is already in the tree (fact F2), cited to the Pennsylvania death certificate source S3, but no research assertion has extracted the parent fields from it. Statewide certificates began in 1906, so the 1908 certificate is the record most likely to name his father (Thomas Flynn) and his mother by name. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 is name-searchable; the original state certificate is held by the Pennsylvania Department of Health, access unknown per the locality entry. Read the parent fields on the certificate itself.

The tree's ParentChild link R1 (Thomas Flynn to Patrick) cites the 1860 census (S2), but no research assertion has been extracted from it. The 1850 link (a_004) is only inferred from household position and shared surname, since the 1850 census does not state relationships. The 1860 census states relationship to head, age and birthplace, so it can confirm Patrick as Thomas's son and may give the mother's given name. United States, Census, 1860 is name-searchable. The 1850 census gives Ireland as Patrick's birthplace (a_002), which conflicts with the objective's Pennsylvania birth, so the 1860 birthplace entry must be read as well.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland) to his wife, which confirms the couple as a unit and, if this was her first marriage, supplies the mother's maiden name. Thomas's birth date sets the earliest possible marriage; the window ends the year before Patrick's birth estimate was complete. Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania, Marriages, 1709-1940 are name-searchable. The marriage proves the union, not that Patrick is their child, so it corroborates rather than establishes parentage. Also check whether the wife married before, since a second surname in later records would show a prior marriage.

Separate item for the Catholic marriage register of Thomas Flynn and his wife, kept at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, which covered Schuylkill until 1961, not at the county. Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 is name-searchable, but its image coverage of the parish may be incomplete, so a parish or archdiocese request may be needed if this is not indexed. A church record may give both parents' names and the bride's origin. It corroborates the couple but does not establish Patrick as their child.

Patrick's baptism, if he was baptised in Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. The birth estimate is ca. 1845 and the tree and 1850 census give Ireland as his birthplace, so a Pennsylvania baptism may not exist; the Irish origin needs its own locality survey before an Irish baptism item can be written. A baptism entry that names both parents places the child with them directly, which is the record that would establish parentage.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, if he died in this window. The window is sized to his lifespan (b. ~1818, so plausibly died 1850-1905), not to the subject's research window. A will or estate file naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence. The Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills and Orphans' Court estate dockets, not a name search. Also search the estate dockets for Thomas's widow and any guardianship of minor children.

FAN item. The 1850 household of Thomas Flynn was dwelling 84 in Schuylkill County (log_001). Its neighbours in the same enumeration, and any Flynn or wife's-family households within a few dwellings, may include the mother's family, a sibling of Patrick, or kin who named Thomas's family in later records. United States, Census, 1850 is name-searchable, so search by the neighbours' surnames rather than by Patrick. What it reveals about Patrick is whether a sibling or the mother's surname appears nearby.

Thomas Flynn's naturalization, if he was naturalised in a Pennsylvania court. His declaration or petition normally gives his birthplace and the year of arrival, which tests the Irish origin of the family and may name a witness who is a FAN lead. Pennsylvania, Eastern District Naturalization Records, 1795-1952 and Pennsylvania, Eastern District Court, Naturalization Records, 1795-1952 are name-searchable. This item gives origin context only; it does not identify parents.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
